subject: business-studies
title: Nature and Scope of Business
meta: Lesson practice set · Question types of the April 2026 NIOS paper
instructions: Practice set for this lesson in the question types of the April 2026 paper.
Where a question has OR, answer either one.
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

questions.answer: D

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an economic activity?
questions.answer: B

questions.q: Which of the following is not a profession?
questions.answer: B

questions.answer: C

questions.answer: B

questions.q: Which of the following is not a feature of a profession?
questions.answer: C

questions.q: Which of the following is not an economic objective of business?
questions.answer: A
questions.note: Creating employment is a social (and national) objective.

questions.answer: D

options: earning maximum profit and ensuring safety of their investment
questions.answer: B

questions.answer: C

sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match, one word or identify).

questions.q: Write True (T) or False (F): (a) It is not always necessary for a businessman to make the best possible use of materials. (b) Businessmen should use profits only for their own living.
questions.answer:
(a) False — best use of resources is an economic objective of business.
(b) False — profits should also be ploughed back for growth and used for the welfare of employees and society.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The economic activity in which one is regularly engaged is called his/her ________. (b) The occupation in which people work for others and earn a fixed income is called ________.
questions.answer:
(a) occupation
(b) employment

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) Activities performed with the objective of earning money are known as ________ activities. (b) The terms and conditions of employment are decided by the ________.
questions.answer:
(a) economic
(b) employer

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) Today, because of ________, the whole world has become a big market. (b) Paying taxes to the government honestly and regularly is a responsibility of business towards the ________.
questions.answer:
(a) globalisation (e-commerce)
(b) government

questions.q: Give an example of an activity which at one time is economic and at another time non-economic.
questions.answer:
(a) A doctor treating patients in her clinic for a fee — economic.
(b) The same doctor treating her own child at home — non-economic.

questions.q: Write True (T) or False (F): (a) A profession requires specialised knowledge and training. (b) Regularity of dealings is not necessary for an activity to be called business.
questions.answer:
(a) True
(b) False — business requires regular dealings.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Mamta sold some rare books to a friend for ₹4,000 and made a profit of ₹1,000. Can this be called business?
questions.answer: No. Business needs regularity of dealings. Mamta sold the books only once, so although she earned a profit, it is not business.

questions.q: Explain the term 'profession' and give two examples.
questions.answer: A profession is an occupation that renders specialised personal services which need special knowledge and training, for a fee, and is regulated by a professional body with a code of conduct. Examples: doctor (Medical Council), lawyer (Bar Council), chartered accountant (ICAI).

questions.q: What is meant by social objectives of business? State any two.
questions.answer: Social objectives are the goals business pursues for the benefit of society. Any two: supplying quality goods at fair prices; avoiding unfair practices like hoarding and misleading advertising; generating employment; paying taxes honestly.

or.q: State any three responsibilities of business towards investors.
or.answer: Ensuring the safety of their money; giving a regular and fair return; giving true and timely information about the company's financial position and plans.

questions.q: Give two examples each of economic and non-economic activities.
questions.answer:
Economic: a teacher teaching in a school for a salary; a shopkeeper selling goods.
Non-economic: a mother cooking for her family; a person doing charity or social service.

questions.q: How can business control pollution? Explain two of its roles.
questions.answer:
Preventive role: use clean technology and treat smoke and effluents before release so that pollution does not occur.
Curative role: repair the damage already caused — clean up rivers and land, plant trees.
(Awareness role: educate employees and the public about pollution.)

questions.q: State any three responsibilities of business towards creditors (suppliers).
questions.answer: Giving regular orders; making payment on time; dealing with them fairly and honestly (fair terms, no undue pressure).

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: State any three features of business.
questions.answer: (1) Dealing in goods and services — producing or buying them for sale. (2) Regularity — dealings must be regular, not a one-time sale. (3) Profit motive — the main aim is to earn profit. (4) Risk and uncertainty — the return is never certain. (Any three.)

questions.q: What is business? Explain any two characteristics of business.
questions.answer:
Business is a regular activity of producing or buying goods and services for sale, transfer or exchange with the object of earning profit.
(1) Sale or exchange: goods are produced for others — making for oneself is not business.
(2) Risk and uncertainty: a businessman invests capital but the return is uncertain because of changes in demand, competition, etc.

or.q: What is water pollution? Explain any two causes.
or.answer:
Water pollution is contamination of water by unwanted and harmful substances that make it unfit for use.
Causes: (1) drainage of human excreta and sewage into rivers and canals; (2) dumping of industrial wastes and effluents; (3) run-off of fertilisers, chemicals and pesticides from fields. (Any two.)

questions.q: Differentiate between economic and non-economic activities on the basis of purpose, outcome and expectation.
questions.answer:
Purpose: economic activities aim to earn money; non-economic activities aim at satisfaction (love, social or religious feeling).
Outcome: economic activities produce income and wealth; non-economic activities give personal satisfaction.
Expectation: in economic activities a monetary return is expected; in non-economic activities no return is expected.

questions.q: Explain any three types of non-economic activities you see around you.
questions.answer:
(1) Social/charitable — helping flood victims, blood donation.
(2) Religious — visiting a temple, serving at a gurdwara langar.
(3) Family and personal — a mother cooking for the family, playing games for recreation.

questions.q: What is air pollution? State three impacts of it.
questions.answer:
Air pollution is contamination of the air by smoke, dust and harmful gases from factories, vehicles and burning of fuels.
Impacts: breathing diseases such as asthma and bronchitis; acid rain that damages buildings and crops; global warming and climate change.

questions.q: Explain the preventive and curative role of business in controlling environmental pollution.
questions.answer:
Preventive: avoid pollution at the source — use clean fuels and technology, install treatment plants for waste water and filters for smoke, follow pollution laws.
Curative: undo damage already done — clean polluted rivers and land, plant trees, recycle waste.
(Awareness: educate employees and the public.)

sections.title: Long answer questions, including case-based questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain any four economic objectives of business.
questions.answer:
(1) Earning profit — profit is essential for survival and growth and is the reward for risk.
(2) Creating customers — profit comes only when goods are sold, so business must attract and satisfy customers by offering the right products at the right price.
(3) Regular innovation — introducing new products, designs and methods to cut costs and beat competition.
(4) Best possible use of resources — using men, materials, machines and money efficiently so that nothing is wasted and costs stay low.

questions.q: What are national objectives of business? Explain four of them.
questions.answer:
National objectives are goals business pursues for the progress of the country.
(1) Generating employment for the people.
(2) Promoting social justice — equal opportunity to all, help to weaker sections.
(3) Producing according to national priorities — goods needed by the nation, as in the plans.
(4) Contributing to government revenue by paying taxes honestly; also self-sufficiency and export promotion.

questions.q: Explain any four responsibilities of business towards owners, and any three towards employees.
questions.answer:
Owners: (1) a fair return on their investment; (2) safety of their capital; (3) efficient and honest management; (4) accurate and timely information about the business.
Employees: (1) fair wages and salaries on time; (2) safe and healthy working conditions; (3) welfare facilities, training and chances of promotion.

questions.q: Distinguish between business, profession and employment on any five bases.
questions.answer:
Mode of establishment: business — entrepreneur's decision and legal formalities; profession — membership of a professional body; employment — appointment letter.
Nature of work: business — goods and services to the public; profession — specialised personal services; employment — work as assigned by the employer.
Qualification: business — none required; profession — special knowledge and training; employment — as prescribed by the employer.
Reward: business — profit; profession — fee; employment — salary or wages.
Capital: business — needed as per size; profession — limited; employment — none.
Risk: business — high; profession — low; employment — none.

questions.q: Explain any three social and any three global objectives of business.
questions.answer:
Social: (1) supplying goods of desired quality at fair prices; (2) avoiding unfair trade practices such as hoarding and misleading advertisements; (3) generating employment and contributing to social welfare.
Global: (1) raising the general standard of living by making quality goods available; (2) reducing disparities among nations through trade and investment; (3) making globally competitive goods and services available.
